Contrite

/kən-TRYT/ — rhymes with incite · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is contrite feels real guilt and sorrow for something wrong they did, and often wants to make up for it.

The contrite student apologized to the librarian and offered to repair the torn book.

Worked Example

After a fight, the boy realized he'd hurt his best friend deeply. Truly ashamed, he showed up at her house with an apology written in his own hand, offered to help with her homework all summer to make amends, and meant every word — a contrite gesture born of genuine remorse.

Contrite is far more precise than just 'sorry.' It means not just regret, but deep, genuine guilt paired with a real desire to fix what you broke and make things right. Saying someone is contrite tells us their remorse is authentic and they're motivated to repair harm.

How Contrite Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sorry

sorry: the everyday word for feeling apologetic

remorseful

remorseful: troubled by deep guilt over harm done

penitent

penitent: sorrowful and solemnly seeking to atone

Antonyms

unrepentant

unrepentant: feeling no guilt at all for wrongdoing

defiant

defiant: boldly refusing to admit any fault

How Strong Is It? — regretful → guilty → contrite → penitent

regretful vs. contrite

regretful vs. contrite: Regretful is weaker than contrite — a regretful person wishes something hadn't happened, while a contrite person feels genuine guilt and wants to repair the damage.

guilty vs. contrite

guilty vs. contrite: Feeling guilty is weaker than being contrite; guilt is the uncomfortable weight of knowing you did wrong, while contrite adds real sorrow and a drive to make amends.

penitent vs. contrite

penitent vs. contrite: Penitent is as strong as contrite, or a shade stronger — both feel deep guilt, but penitent adds a solemn, almost religious commitment to atone.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of contrite.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together; thoroughly (intensive) (Latin)

Root — trit

Root — trit: rubbed, ground down (from terere, 'to rub, grind') (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin contritus means 'thoroughly ground down or worn to pieces' — con- ('thoroughly') plus terere/tritus ('to rub, grind'). A contrite person is crushed and ground down by guilt over what they did.

Use the root in a new word: trite

Use the root in a new word: trite: A trite excuse is one worn out and 'ground down' by overuse — the same grinding root, terere, that leaves a contrite person crushed by guilt.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / somewhat literary

Contrite is stronger and more serious than 'sorry.' Use it when someone shows genuine, deep guilt and a clear drive to repair harm — not just polite regret or an apology made to escape trouble. Reserve it for true remorse and a sincere effort to make things right.
